About this guide

The new Verbal Ability section has three timed tasks: Sentence Completion (20 items, about 25 seconds each), Passage Recall (4 tasks, 30 seconds to read and 90 seconds to type) and Email Writing (about 9 minutes). This guide teaches the grammar and vocabulary behind the first task from zero, then trains the memory and writing skills for the other two.

How each chapter is built

  • Idea: the topic in plain words.
  • Diagram: a picture of the method.
  • Rules box: the yellow box to revise.
  • Solved examples with the reason for the answer.
  • Shortcuts and mistakes.
  • Practice set (Basic, Medium, Advanced) with answers at the end.

How to study

  • Chapters 1–12: one or two a day; redo the examples without looking.
  • Chapter 13: timed drills at 25 seconds per item.
  • Chapter 14: practise recall with a timer and score the key facts.
  • Chapter 15: write one email a day from the templates.
  • Chapter 16: take the mini test and follow the five-week plan.

VERBAL ABILITY · FOUNDATION · START HERE

Parts of Speech and Sentence Basics

Every sentence-completion question is built from a few simple parts. Before you learn tenses and agreement, be sure you can name each word’s job. Once you can say “this blank needs a verb” or “this blank needs an adjective”, wrong options vanish quickly.
Eight parts of speech. A word can change its job with its place in the sentence: “light” is a noun in “turn on the light”, an adjective in “a light bag” and a verb in “light a lamp”.
A sentence has a subject (who or what), a verb (what happens) and often an object (who or what receives the action).

Basic rules

  • A complete sentence needs a subject and a finite verb and must express a complete thought.
  • Noun forms: singular/plural (child–children), countable/uncountable (bottle/water), common/proper (city/Mumbai).
  • Adjective goes before a noun (a quick reply) or after a linking verb (the reply was quick).
  • Adverb answers how, when, where or how much (replied quickly, arrived late, very tall).
  • Preposition is followed by a noun or pronoun (in the office, with him), and by the -ing form of a verb (good at singing).
  • Conjunctions: coordinating (FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so), subordinating (because, although, if, when, while).
  • Transitive verbs need an object (she reads books); intransitive verbs do not (she sleeps).
Word-ending hintUsually aExamples
-tion, -ment, -ness, -ity, -ancenounaction, payment, kindness, ability
-ful, -ous, -able, -ive, -aladjectivecareful, famous, readable, active
-ly (added to adjective)adverbquickly, carefully
-ize, -ify, -en, -ateverborganize, simplify, widen, create
Choose the word that fits: Her ___ to the project was appreciated. (a) contribute (b) contribution (c) contributing (d) contributory
(b) contribution
The blank follows “Her” and is the subject, so a noun is needed: contribution. Suffix -tion marks a noun.
Choose the word that fits: He answered the question ___. (a) correct (b) correctness (c) correctly (d) correcting
(c) correctly
A word is needed to describe how he answered, so an adverb: correctly.
Identify the part of speech of “fast” in: He is a fast learner.
Adjective
“Fast” describes the noun “learner”.

Shortcuts and tricks

  • Look at the word before and after the blank; it decides the part of speech.
  • A blank after an article (a/an/the) or an adjective is usually a noun.
  • A blank after “is / was / are” can be an adjective or a verb in -ing/-ed.
  • A blank before an adjective is usually an adverb (very, quite, extremely).

Common mistakes

  • Using an adjective where an adverb is needed (“he runs quick”).
  • Using a noun where an adjective is needed (“a success plan” instead of “a successful plan”).
  • Using a verb after a preposition without -ing (“interested in learn”).

Practice set: Foundation practice

VERBAL ABILITY · GRAMMAR · MUST-DO

Tenses

A tense tells when an action happens and whether it is finished or still going. It is the most common blank in sentence completion. Learn the twelve forms as a table and learn the signal words that point to each one.
Every tense is a combination of time (past, present, future) and type (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous).
Where each tense sits relative to “now”.
TenseUseSignal wordsExample
Simple presenthabit, fact, schedulealways, every day, usually, neverShe goes to office by metro.
Present continuoushappening now / planned soonnow, at the moment, today, currentlyThey are waiting outside.
Present perfectpast action with present resultsince, for, already, yet, just, ever, so farI have finished the report.
Present perfect continuousaction started in past and still goingsince, for, how long, latelyHe has been working since 9 a.m.
Simple pastfinished action at a known timeyesterday, ago, last week, in 2019We met last Monday.
Past continuousaction in progress at a past momentwhile, when, at that timeI was sleeping when you called.
Past perfectearlier of two past actionsbefore, after, by the time, alreadyThe train had left when we arrived.
Simple futuredecision, predictiontomorrow, soon, next weekI will call you.
Future perfectfinished before a future timeby next month, by thenBy June she will have graduated.

Rules to remember

  • since + point of time (since 2020); for + period (for five years). Both go with present perfect (not simple past).
  • After if / when / before / after / as soon as / unless / until referring to the future, use the present tense, not “will”: “If it rains, we will stay.”
  • By the time + simple past, main clause in past perfect: “By the time we arrived, the show had started.”
  • Just now / ago / yesterday / last year → simple past (never present perfect).
  • Stative verbs (know, like, want, believe, own, belong) are normally not used in continuous forms.
  • Reported speech: tense moves one step back (is → was, has done → had done). Universal truths stay in simple present.
  • Sequence of tenses: keep the tense consistent in one narrative unless the time really changes.
He ___ in this company since 2018. (a) works (b) worked (c) has worked (d) is working
(c) has worked
“Since 2018” links the past to the present, so present perfect.
By the time the manager arrived, the meeting ___. (a) ended (b) has ended (c) had ended (d) was ending
(c) had ended
Two past events: the meeting ended earlier, so past perfect.
If she ___ hard, she will pass the exam. (a) will work (b) works (c) worked (d) would work
(b) works
After “if” in a future condition use the simple present.
I ___ him yesterday. (a) have met (b) met (c) had met (d) meet
(b) met
“Yesterday” fixes a finished time: simple past.
The teacher said that the earth ___ round the sun. (a) moved (b) moves (c) had moved (d) was moving
(b) moves
A universal truth stays in the simple present even in reported speech.

Shortcuts and tricks

  • Underline the time word first; it decides the tense in about 80% of questions.
  • Two past events: earlier = past perfect, later = simple past.
  • “Since / for / already / yet / just / ever” → present perfect.
  • “Yesterday / ago / last / in 2015” → simple past.
  • After “wish” use a past form: “I wish I knew the answer.”

Common mistakes

  • Simple past with “since” or “for” (“I lived here since 2019”).
  • “Will” inside an if-clause (“If it will rain”).
  • Present perfect with a finished time word (“I have seen him yesterday”).
  • Continuous with stative verbs (“I am knowing him”).

Practice set: Tenses practice

2.They ___ a movie now. (a) watch (b) watched (c) are watching (d) have watchedBasic

VERBAL ABILITY · GRAMMAR · MUST-DO

Subject–Verb Agreement

A verb must agree with its subject in number. The trick is to find the real subject, because the exam puts extra words between the subject and the verb to confuse you.
Three moves for every agreement question.

The agreement rules

  • Each, every, either, neither, one of, none of + singular verb: “Each of the boys has a pen.”
  • Along with, together with, as well as, in addition to: verb agrees with the first subject: “The CEO, along with his staff, is present.”
  • Either … or / neither … nor / not only … but also: verb agrees with the nearer subject: “Neither the manager nor the employees are ready.”
  • And joins two subjects → plural: “Rama and Sita are friends.” Exception: one idea or one person: “Bread and butter is my breakfast.”
  • Collective nouns (team, committee, family, jury) → singular when acting as one group, plural when members act separately.
  • Uncountable nouns (information, advice, furniture, news, luggage, equipment, knowledge) are singular: “The news is good.”
  • Plural-looking singular words: mathematics, physics, economics, news, series, measles → singular. Scissors, trousers, glasses, jeans → plural.
  • A phrase of measure (money, time, distance) → singular: “Ten kilometres is a long way.”
  • The number of + plural noun → singular verb; A number of + plural noun → plural verb.
  • There is / There are: the verb agrees with the noun that follows.
  • Relative clause: “He is one of those who are late.” (verb agrees with “those”).
Neither of the answers ___ correct. (a) are (b) is (c) were (d) be
(b) is
“Neither of” takes a singular verb.
The manager, along with his team, ___ attending the meeting. (a) are (b) is (c) were (d) have been
(b) is
Real subject is “manager”; “along with his team” is ignored.
A number of students ___ absent today. (a) is (b) was (c) are (d) has been
(c) are
“A number of” + plural noun gives a plural verb.
The number of unemployed graduates ___ rising. (a) are (b) have been (c) is (d) were
(c) is
“The number of” is singular (it refers to the count).
Either the teacher or the students ___ responsible. (a) is (b) are (c) was (d) has been
(b) are
Verb agrees with the nearer subject “students”.

Shortcuts and tricks

  • Cross out everything between commas or inside “of …” phrases and read the sentence again.
  • Singular words that look plural: news, economics, mathematics.
  • For “either … or”, look at the word nearest the verb.
  • “Many a” takes a singular verb: “Many a man has tried.”

Common mistakes

  • Agreeing the verb with the nearest noun instead of the real subject (“The box of apples are fresh”).
  • Treating “news” and “information” as plural.
  • Using plural after “each / every”.

Practice set: Agreement practice

1.Each of the players ___ a medal. (a) have received (b) has received (c) are receiving (d) were receiveBasic
2.The news ___ true. (a) are (b) is (c) were (d) have beenBasic
3.Neither the captain nor the players ___ ready. (a) is (b) was (c) are (d) hasMedium
4.The team ___ practising together. (a) is (b) are (c) were (d) beMedium
5.Mathematics ___ my favourite subject. (a) are (b) is (c) were (d) have beenMedium
6.The quality of these mangoes ___ poor. (a) are (b) is (c) were (d) have beenAdvanced
7.One of the boys who ___ late was punished. (a) was (b) is (c) were (d) has beenAdvanced

VERBAL ABILITY · GRAMMAR · IMPORTANT

Articles and Determiners

Articles (a, an, the) and determiners (some, any, much, many, few, little, this, those) show which noun or how many. Questions test sound-based “a/an”, the use of “the” with unique things, and the difference between few/a few and little/a little.
Follow the tree from the top. The sound, not the spelling, decides a or an.

Rules

  • a / an: first mention, one of many. an before a vowel sound (an hour, an umbrella); a before a consonant sound (a university, a European).
  • the: a noun already known, unique (the sun, the moon, the Earth), a superlative (the best), an ordinal (the first), rivers, oceans, mountain ranges (the Ganga, the Himalayas), newspapers (The Hindu), some countries (the USA, the UK).
  • No article: plural/uncountable nouns used generally (Dogs are loyal; Water is essential), most countries and cities (India, Pune), languages, subjects (Maths), meals (have lunch), most sports.
  • Few / a few (countable): few = almost none (negative); a few = some (positive). Little / a little (uncountable): same idea.
  • Much + uncountable; many + countable. Fewer + countable; less + uncountable.
  • Some in positive sentences and offers; any in negatives and questions.
  • Each / every / either / neither + singular noun; both / few / many + plural noun.
  • Fixed phrases: in the morning, on the whole, by the way, at the moment; by bus, at home, in bed, at school (no article).
She is ___ honest girl. (a) a (b) an (c) the (d) no article
(b) an
“Honest” begins with a silent h; the sound is a vowel sound.
He bought ___ umbrella and ___ bag. ___ umbrella was red. (a) an, a, The (b) a, an, An (c) an, the, A (d) the, a, An
(a) an, a, The
First mention: an umbrella, a bag; second mention: The umbrella.
There is ___ water left in the bottle. We can hardly drink. (a) few (b) a few (c) little (d) a little
(c) little
Water is uncountable; “hardly” makes the sense negative, so “little”.
The Ganga is ___ longest river in India. (a) a (b) an (c) the (d) no article
(c) the
Superlative takes “the”.
“There are ___ students in the class this year.” (a) less (b) fewer (c) much (d) little
(b) fewer
Students are countable.

Shortcuts and tricks

  • Say the word aloud: a unit, an hour, an MBA, a one-way street.
  • Superlative or ordinal in the blank → “the”.
  • “few” and “little” are negative; add “a” to make them positive.
  • Plural and uncountable nouns used in general statements take no article.

Common mistakes

  • “an university” (sound is “you”).
  • “the” before a general plural (“The dogs are loyal” as a general fact).
  • “less” with countable nouns.

Practice set: Article practice

1.He is ___ European. (a) a (b) an (c) the (d) no articleBasic
2.I met ___ old man yesterday. (a) a (b) an (c) the (d) no articleBasic
3.___ Sun rises in the east. (a) A (b) An (c) The (d) No articleBasic
4.We have ___ time to finish. (a) few (b) a few (c) little (d) manyMedium
5.He plays ___ cricket every evening. (a) a (b) an (c) the (d) no articleMedium
6.She was ___ only candidate selected. (a) a (b) an (c) the (d) no articleMedium
7.There are ___ people in the hall than yesterday. (a) less (b) fewer (c) much (d) littleAdvanced
8.He has ___ few friends, so he feels lonely. (a) a (b) an (c) the (d) —Advanced

Prepositions

Prepositions are small words with a big share of marks. There is no logic behind many of them, so the strategy is to learn the time and place rules and then memorise the common dependent prepositions (adjective + preposition, verb + preposition).
The in-on-at funnel for time and the space-surface-point idea for place.
Adjective + prepositionVerb + prepositionNoun + preposition
good at, bad at, weak independ on, rely on, insist onreason for, need for
afraid of, fond of, proud of, capable oflook for (search), look after (care), look into (investigate)cause of, solution to, answer to
angry with (person), angry at (thing)agree with (person), agree to (proposal), agree on (matter)interest in, increase in, demand for
famous for, responsible for, eligible forapologise to (person) for (action)difference between, relation between
married to, similar to, superior to, senior toprevent … from, protect … fromaccess to, attitude towards

Rules

  • since + point of time, for + period of time.
  • between two things, among more than two.
  • beside = next to; besides = in addition to.
  • in / within: “within a week” = before a week ends; “in a week” = after a week.
  • by = not later than (by Friday) or the agent (written by him); until / till = up to a time.
  • on a bus / train / plane / bike; in a car / taxi.
  • After a preposition use a noun, pronoun or -ing form: “She is good at dancing.”
  • Prepositions are not used before: tomorrow, yesterday, today, last, next, this (e.g., “next week”, not “on next week”).
He has been working here ___ 2019. (a) for (b) from (c) since (d) in
(c) since
2019 is a point of time.
She is very fond ___ music. (a) with (b) of (c) at (d) on
(b) of
Fixed phrase: fond of.
The prize was divided ___ the three winners. (a) between (b) among (c) in (d) with
(b) among
More than two persons: among.
The report must be submitted ___ Friday at the latest. (a) in (b) at (c) by (d) since
(c) by
“By” marks a deadline: not later than Friday.
The meeting starts ___ 10 a.m. ___ Monday. (a) in, on (b) at, on (c) at, in (d) on, at
(b) at, on
Clock time: at; day: on.

Shortcuts and tricks

  • Learn adjectives with their preposition as a pair: fond of, good at, afraid of.
  • For time: in (big), on (day), at (clock).
  • For travel: on a bus, in a car.
  • When two prepositions fit, choose the one used with the main word (collocation), not the one that “sounds” right.

Common mistakes

  • “depend from”, “discuss about”, “enter into the room”, “married with”: all wrong.
  • Using “among” for two persons.
  • Using “since” with a period (“since two years”).

3.The book is ___ the table. (a) in (b) on (c) at (d) byBasic

VERBAL ABILITY · GRAMMAR · IMPORTANT

Pronouns and Conjunctions

A pronoun replaces a noun; a conjunction joins words or clauses. Pronoun questions test case (I/me), agreement and reflexives. Conjunction questions test the logical link between two ideas: addition, contrast, reason, result.
The full pronoun table. Subject form comes before the verb, object form after a verb or preposition.

Pronoun rules

  • After a preposition use the object form: between you and me (not “between you and I”), with him.
  • After than / as, finish the sentence mentally: “She is taller than I (am).”
  • Who = subject (who did it), whom = object (to whom, whom did you see). Whose = possession.
  • Reflexive (myself …) is used when subject and object are the same or for emphasis: “She hurt herself.” Do not use it as a subject.
  • A pronoun must agree with its noun in number and person: “Each student must bring his or her ID card.”
  • One … one’s; everyone / someone / nobody → singular pronoun (he or she / they as a common form).
  • Its (possessive, no apostrophe) vs it’s (it is / it has).
  • Relative pronouns: who (people), which (things), that (people or things, restrictive), whose (possession).
Choose the connector by the relationship between the two ideas.

Conjunction rules

  • Although / though / even though + clause (no “but” in the same sentence): “Although he was tired, he finished the work.”
  • Despite / in spite of + noun or -ing (not a full clause): “Despite the rain, …”
  • Because + clause; because of / due to / owing to + noun.
  • Unless = if not (do not use “not” after unless).
  • Not only … but also, both … and, either … or, neither … nor must be followed by the same grammatical form (parallel).
  • Hardly / scarcely … when, no sooner … than: “No sooner had he arrived than it rained.”
  • Lest + should: “Work hard lest you should fail.”
  • While can show time or contrast; whereas shows contrast.
She is taller than ___. (a) I (b) me (c) myself (d) mine
(a) I
“Than I am”: subject form after than.
The decision was taken between my manager and ___. (a) I (b) me (c) myself (d) mine
(b) me
After a preposition: object form.
___ it was raining, the match continued. (a) Because (b) Although (c) Unless (d) So
(b) Although
The match continuing is a contrast to the rain.
He was tired ___ he went to bed early. (a) but (b) so (c) although (d) unless
(b) so
Result: tired, therefore went to bed.
You will not succeed ___ you work hard. (a) if (b) unless (c) although (d) until
(b) unless
Unless = if not.

Shortcuts and tricks

  • Test a pronoun by removing the other person: “between you and (I/me)” → “between me”.
  • If the two ideas are opposite, choose a contrast word; if one causes the other, choose a reason/result word.
  • Do not use two connectors for one idea (“Although … but …” is wrong).
  • Read the sentence with your option; if the logic breaks, reject it.

Common mistakes

  • “Between you and I”, “for him and I”.
  • “Despite of”, “inspite”.
  • “Because of” followed by a clause.
  • Using “myself” as a subject (“Myself and Raj went”).

Practice set: Pronoun and conjunction practice

2.This book is ___. (a) my (b) me (c) mine (d) myselfBasic
3.___ he was ill, he came to work. (a) Because (b) Although (c) Unless (d) SoBasic
4.The man ___ car was stolen filed a complaint. (a) who (b) whom (c) whose (d) whichMedium
5.He failed ___ he did not study. (a) although (b) because (c) unless (d) butMedium
6.___ the heavy traffic, we reached on time. (a) Although (b) Despite (c) Because (d) UnlessMedium
7.No sooner had she entered ___ the lights went off. (a) when (b) than (c) then (d) thatAdvanced
8.The cat licked ___ paws. (a) it’s (b) its (c) their (d) hisAdvanced

VERBAL ABILITY · GRAMMAR · IMPORTANT

Adjectives, Adverbs and Comparison

Adjectives describe nouns; adverbs describe verbs, adjectives or other adverbs. Comparison questions test the correct degree (good–better–best), the word than, and double comparatives.
Positive, comparative and superlative.
PositiveComparativeSuperlativeRule
talltallertallestone syllable: add -er / -est
happyhappierhappiesty → i + er / est
beautifulmore beautifulmost beautifullong words: more / most
goodbetterbestirregular
badworseworstirregular
farfarther / furtherfarthest / furthestdistance / extra
oldolder / elderoldest / eldestelder, eldest only for family
littlelessleastirregular
much / manymoremostirregular

Rules

  • Use than with the comparative, never “then” or “from”. Exceptions: senior to, junior to, superior to, inferior to, prefer … to use “to”.
  • No double comparatives or superlatives: “more better”, “most unkindest” are wrong.
  • The superlative takes “the” and is used with three or more things: “the tallest of the three”.
  • Adverbs of manner usually end in -ly; good → well, fast → fast, hard → hard (hardly means almost not).
  • Adjective order: opinion → size → age → shape → colour → origin → material: “a beautiful small old round red Indian wooden box”.
  • Enough goes after an adjective (tall enough) and before a noun (enough money).
  • Very + positive (very good); much + comparative (much better); too = more than needed (too hot to drink).
  • Latin comparatives (senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior, anterior) take to.
  • Absolute adjectives are not compared: unique, perfect, complete, round, empty, dead.
This is the ___ book I have ever read. (a) good (b) better (c) best (d) more good
(c) best
“the … ever” needs a superlative; good → best.
He is senior ___ me. (a) than (b) to (c) from (d) of
(b) to
Senior takes “to”.
She works ___ than her sister. (a) hard (b) harder (c) hardest (d) hardly
(b) harder
“than” needs a comparative.
He is ___ to carry the box. (a) enough strong (b) strong enough (c) too strong (d) so strong
(b) strong enough
Enough follows the adjective.

Shortcuts and tricks

  • Look for “than” (comparative) or “the … of / in” (superlative) before choosing.
  • Never double: “more better” is wrong.
  • “to” after senior / junior / superior / inferior / prefer.
  • If the adjective is long (three syllables or more), use more / most.

Common mistakes

  • “more better”, “most easiest”.
  • “He is more taller than me.”
  • “He is elder than me” (use “older than” unless family relation; “elder to” is wrong).

Practice set: Comparison practice

VERBAL ABILITY · GRAMMAR · IMPORTANT

Modals, Conditionals and Wishes

Modal verbs (can, may, must, should) show ability, permission, duty and possibility. Conditionals link a condition to a result. Both appear often in sentence completion because each pattern has a fixed shape.
Match the if-clause tense to the main clause tense.
ModalMeaningExample
can / couldability, possibilityShe can swim. Could you help me?
may / mightpermission, possibilityMay I come in? It might rain.
muststrong necessity / strong deductionYou must wear a helmet. He must be at home.
should / ought toadvice, dutyYou should sleep early.
have toexternal obligationI have to submit it today.
used topast habitShe used to play chess.
wouldpolite request, past habitWould you wait? He would visit every Sunday.
need notno necessityYou need not come.

Rules

  • After a modal use the base verb (no -s, no to, no -ing): “She can sing.”
  • If I were (not “was”) in unreal present conditions: “If I were you, …”.
  • Had + subject + V3 can replace “if”: “Had I known, I would have come.”
  • Should + subject + V1 can replace “if”: “Should you need help, call me.”
  • I wish + past (present regret); I wish + had + V3 (past regret): “I wish I had studied.”
  • Would rather + V1 (I would rather stay); would rather + subject + past (I would rather you stayed).
  • Used to + V1 (past habit); be used to + V-ing (accustomed): “I am used to waking early.”
  • Had better + V1 = advice: “You had better leave now.”
  • Suggest / insist / demand + (that) + subject + V1 or should: “He insisted that she go.”
If I ___ you, I would accept the offer. (a) am (b) was (c) were (d) will be
(c) were
Second conditional uses “were” for all persons.
If he had worked harder, he ___ the exam. (a) will pass (b) would pass (c) would have passed (d) passed
(c) would have passed
Third conditional: past perfect → would have + V3.
I would rather ___ at home. (a) stay (b) to stay (c) staying (d) stayed
(a) stay
Would rather + base verb.
She is used to ___ early. (a) wake (b) waking (c) woke (d) woken
(b) waking
Be used to + V-ing means accustomed to.
Hardly ___ the office when it started raining. (a) he left (b) had he left (c) he had left (d) did he leave
(b) had he left
Hardly takes inversion with past perfect: had he left … when.

Shortcuts and tricks

  • Identify the if-clause tense and pick the matching main clause.
  • “Would” never appears in the if-clause of a conditional.
  • Modal + base verb: remove -s, to and -ing.
  • “Had I …, I would have …” is the third conditional without “if”.

Common mistakes

  • “If it will rain”.
  • “If I was you” (use were in formal English).
  • “She can to swim”, “He must goes”.
  • “I wish I would have known”.

VERBAL ABILITY · GRAMMAR · IMPORTANT

Active–Passive Voice and Reported Speech

Voice changes who is in focus (doer or receiver). Reported speech retells what someone said. Both topics follow a mechanical pattern: learn the pattern and the answer follows.
Active ↔ passive. The object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive.
TenseActivePassive
Simple presentShe writes a letter.A letter is written by her.
Present continuousShe is writing a letter.A letter is being written by her.
Present perfectShe has written a letter.A letter has been written by her.
Simple pastShe wrote a letter.A letter was written by her.
Past continuousShe was writing a letter.A letter was being written by her.
Past perfectShe had written a letter.A letter had been written by her.
Simple futureShe will write a letter.A letter will be written by her.
ModalShe can write a letter.A letter can be written by her.

Passive voice rules

  • Passive = be (in the right tense) + past participle.
  • Only transitive verbs have a passive form (no passive for “arrive”, “sleep”).
  • Questions: “Who wrote it?” → “By whom was it written?”
  • Imperative: “Open the door.” → “Let the door be opened.”
  • Reported speech: tense steps back; pronouns and time words change (see table).
  • Questions in reported speech: asked + if / whether (yes/no) or asked + wh-word, statement word order (no question inversion): “He asked me where I lived.”
  • Commands become to-infinitives: “She told me to sit.” Requests: “asked me to”. Advice: “advised me to”.
  • Statements use said that / told (someone) that.
  • Facts that are always true keep the present: “He said that the sun rises in the east.”
Tense and word shifts for indirect speech.
Change to passive: “They are repairing the road.”
The road is being repaired.
Present continuous: is / are being + V3.
Change to passive: “Who wrote this letter?”
By whom was this letter written?
Simple past passive of a question.
Change to indirect speech: He said, “I am tired.”
He said that he was tired.
Present continuous “am” steps back to “was”; “I” becomes “he”.
Change to indirect speech: She asked, “Where do you live?”
She asked where I lived.
Statement order, past tense, pronoun change.
Change to indirect speech: The teacher said, “Close the door.”
The teacher ordered / told us to close the door.
Imperative becomes a to-infinitive.

Shortcuts and tricks

  • Passive: find the object, make it the subject, add the right form of be + V3.
  • Reported questions have no “do / does / did” and no question mark.
  • If the reporting verb is in the present (“He says”), the tense does not shift.
  • Time words move: now → then, today → that day, ago → before.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting “been” in perfect passives (“has written by”).
  • Keeping question word order in reported questions.
  • Using “that” before a question or command.

Practice set: Voice and speech practice

4.She said, “I am cooking.” → She said that she ___. (a) is cooking (b) was cooking (c) has been cooking (d) cookedMedium
5.He asked, “Are you ready?” → He asked ___. (a) if I was ready (b) are you ready (c) that I was ready (d) if was I readyMedium
6.Passive of “Someone is watching us.” (a) We are watched. (b) We are being watched. (c) We were watched. (d) We have been watched.Medium
7.Passive of “Open the window.” (a) The window is open. (b) Let the window be opened. (c) The window should open. (d) The window opened.Advanced
8.The mother said to her son, “Do not play here.” → The mother ___ here. (a) told her son not to play (b) said her son not to play (c) told her son do not play (d) asked her son to not playedAdvanced

Vocabulary and Word Choice

Vocabulary questions ask which word best fits the meaning and tone of the sentence. You do not need thousands of rare words; you need word roots, the most common synonym/antonym groups, confusing pairs and collocations.
Break an unknown word into prefix, root and suffix to guess its meaning.
PrefixMeaningExamples
un-, in-, im-, il-, ir-, dis-, non-not / oppositeunhappy, incorrect, impossible, illegal, irregular, disagree

Frequently confused words

PairDifference
affect / effectaffect (verb) = influence; effect (noun) = result

One-word substitutions and collocations

PhraseOne word
a person who knows everythingomniscient
one who does not believe in Godatheist

Collocations (words that go together)

  • make a decision, make a mistake, make progress; do homework, do business, do a favour
  • take a risk, take a chance, take advantage of; give advice, give a speech, give priority
  • heavy rain, strong tea, high temperature, deep sleep, fast food
  • meet a deadline, conduct a survey, launch a product, draw a conclusion
  • commit a crime, pay attention, run a business, lay the foundation
The speaker’s ___ speech kept the audience hooked. (a) monotonous (b) captivating (c) vague (d) tedious
(b) captivating
“Kept hooked” needs a positive word: captivating means attractive and engaging.
Choose the synonym of “scarce”. (a) abundant (b) rare (c) common (d) plentiful
(b) rare
Scarce means little available, so rare.
Choose the antonym of “benevolent”. (a) kind (b) malevolent (c) generous (d) gentle
(b) malevolent
bene = good, mal = bad.
The new rule will ___ the speed of delivery. (a) effect (b) affect (c) infect (d) defect
(b) affect
A verb is needed (influence): affect.
A speech given without any preparation is called ___. (a) extempore (b) prepared (c) formal (d) oration
(a) extempore
Standard one-word substitution.

Shortcuts and tricks

  • Read the sentence for tone first (positive or negative), then pick the word.
  • Use roots: mal = bad, bene = good, anti = against, pre = before.
  • For synonyms, test by replacing the word in a simple sentence.
  • Learn 10 new words every day with one example sentence each.

Common mistakes

  • Picking a word that is grammatically right but changes the tone of the sentence.
  • Mixing confusing pairs (affect/effect, principal/principle).
  • Choosing a rare, “big” word without checking the meaning.

Idioms and Phrasal Verbs

An idiom is a fixed expression whose meaning is not the sum of its words. A phrasal verb is a verb plus a small word (up, down, off, out) that gives a new meaning. Both must be learnt as units; here are the ones that appear most often.
Idioms are figurative. Never translate them word by word.

Common idioms

IdiomMeaning
a blessing in disguisesomething good that seemed bad at first
bite the bulletface a hard situation bravely
break the icestart a conversation
burn the midnight oilwork late at night
call it a daystop working for now
cost an arm and a legbe very expensive
cut cornersdo something cheaply, skipping steps
get cold feetbecome too nervous to do something
go the extra milemake more effort than expected
hit the nail on the headbe exactly right
in the long runover a long time
once in a blue moonvery rarely
piece of cakevery easy
spill the beansreveal a secret
under the weatherslightly ill
the ball is in your courtit is your turn to act

Common phrasal verbs

Phrasal verbMeaning
call offcancel
carry outperform / execute
come acrossfind by chance
figure outunderstand / solve
give upstop trying
look aftertake care of
look intoinvestigate
look forward towait eagerly for
put offpostpone
put up withtolerate
run out ofhave none left
set upestablish
turn downreject
turn uparrive / appear
take overtake control
bring upraise (a child / topic)

How to learn them

  • Group by verb: look (after, into, up, forward to), turn (down, up, on, off), put (off, up with, out).
  • Write one sentence for each phrase; the sentence builds the memory.
  • Check the object: “turn down an offer” (reject) vs “turn the volume down” (reduce).
  • Idioms are fixed; do not change a word (“a piece of cakes” is wrong).
  • In sentence completion, test each option by replacing the idiom with its plain meaning.
She did not ___ the offer because the salary was low. (a) turn up (b) turn down (c) turn on (d) turn in
(b) turn down
“Reject” is the needed meaning.
The match was ___ due to heavy rain. (a) called off (b) called on (c) called up (d) called in
(a) called off
Called off = cancelled.
He promised to keep it secret but he ___ the beans. (a) spilled (b) dropped (c) threw (d) lost
(a) spilled
Idiom: spill the beans.
We have ___ paper; please order more. (a) run out of (b) run into (c) run over (d) run after
(a) run out of
Run out of = have none left.

Shortcuts and tricks

  • Replace the phrase by a simple word to test meaning: called off = cancelled.
  • Learn by verb groups.
  • For idioms, picture the literal image and the real meaning together.
  • Never change the words of an idiom.

Common mistakes

  • Using “put on” for “postpone” (the right form is put off).
  • Using “look for” (search) for “look after” (care).
  • Adding extra words: “break the ices”.

VERBAL ABILITY · GRAMMAR · IMPORTANT

Error Spotting and Sentence Structure

Error-spotting asks you to find the part of a sentence that is wrong, or to choose the correct sentence among four. The same ten or so errors repeat. A fixed scanning order finds them faster than reading for “sound”.
Check in this order; stop when you find the error.

Frequent structure rules

  • Parallelism: items in a list must have the same form: “She likes reading, writing and painting” (not “to paint”).
  • Misplaced modifier: place the modifier next to what it modifies. Wrong: “Walking down the road, the tree fell.” Right: “While I was walking down the road, a tree fell.”
  • Double negative: “He did not do nothing” is wrong; use “He did nothing.”
  • Redundancy: “return back”, “reverse back”, “repeat again”, “free gift”, “advance planning” repeat the same idea.
  • Run-on / comma splice: two sentences joined only by a comma need a conjunction or full stop.
  • Fragment: a group of words without a main verb is not a sentence (“Because he was late.”).
  • Countable vs uncountable: “furniture, advice, information, luggage” never take “s” or “a”.
  • Plural forms: “he gave me some advice”, not “advices”.
  • Comparison: compare like with like: “The climate of Pune is cooler than that of Delhi.”
  • Verb + gerund / infinitive: enjoy + V-ing, avoid + V-ing, decide + to V, want + to V, suggest + V-ing.
WrongRightRule
He gave me many advices.He gave me much advice.uncountable
She is more taller.She is taller.double comparative
I am knowing him.I know him.stative verb
He suggested me to go.He suggested that I go.suggest + that / V-ing
The team are playing well.The team is playing well.collective noun, one unit
Each of the boys have a pen.Each of the boys has a pen.each + singular
I prefer tea than coffee.I prefer tea to coffee.prefer … to
Though he was tired, but he worked.Though he was tired, he worked.no “but” with though
He is better than me in maths.He is better than I (am) in maths.case after than
Spot the error: “One of my friend (a) / is a doctor (b) / and works in Mumbai (c) / No error (d).”
(a)
“One of” is followed by a plural noun: “one of my friends”.
Spot the error: “He gave me (a) / several advices (b) / on how to study (c) / No error (d).”
(b)
“Advice” is uncountable: “some advice”.
Choose the correct sentence: (a) Neither of the boys are present. (b) Neither of the boys is present. (c) Neither boys is present. (d) Neither of the boy is present.
(b)
“Neither of” + plural noun + singular verb.
Choose the correct sentence: (a) Walking in the park, the sun was bright. (b) While we were walking in the park, the sun was bright. (c) The sun was bright in the park. (d) Walking in the park, we found the sun bright.
(d)
The modifier “Walking in the park” must be next to “we”.

Shortcuts and tricks

  • Read the sentence in four parts and test each part against the checklist.
  • Prepositions and agreement hold most of the errors.
  • If a sentence “sounds fine”, check for a hidden agreement or tense error.
  • If you find nothing after one scan, choose “No error” and move on.

Common mistakes

  • Correcting style instead of grammar.
  • Choosing “No error” without checking the verb and preposition.
  • Missing a pronoun mismatch (“Everyone must bring their pen”—acceptable in modern usage but “his or her” is the exam form).

VERBAL ABILITY · NEW PATTERN TASK 1 · MUST-DO

Sentence Completion: the 25-Second Method

In the new Verbal pattern the first task is sentence completion: 20 items with about 25 seconds each. You see a sentence with a blank and four options. There is no time for long thought, so success comes from a fixed routine plus the grammar and vocabulary you learned in the earlier chapters.
Practise with a timer until the routine runs by itself.
Decide the type of blank in the first 5 seconds. It tells you which rule to apply.

The routine

  • Read once and look at the two words before and after the blank.
  • Type the blank: grammar, vocabulary or logic.
  • Eliminate in this order: verb form → preposition → article/pronoun → connector logic → word meaning.
  • Choose and move. If two options remain, pick the one that keeps the meaning and sounds natural.
  • No negative marking: never leave an item blank.
  • Do not go back to a skipped item; the timer is per item.
  • Mark the questions you got wrong in practice and write the rule in an error log.

Worked examples by blank type

GRAMMAR (tense). By the time we reached the hall, the programme ___. (a) started (b) has started (c) had started (d) starts
(c) had started
“By the time” + past; the earlier action takes past perfect.
GRAMMAR (agreement). The manager, along with his team, ___ attending the meeting. (a) are (b) is (c) were (d) be
(b) is
Subject is “manager”.
GRAMMAR (preposition). She is allergic ___ dust. (a) with (b) of (c) to (d) at
(c) to
Fixed phrase: allergic to.
VOCABULARY (tone). The report was so ___ that nobody could understand the conclusion. (a) concise (b) vague (c) accurate (d) clear
(b) vague
The result (nobody could understand) shows a negative word: vague.
VOCABULARY (collocation). We need to ___ a decision before Friday. (a) do (b) make (c) take up (d) give
(b) make
Collocation: make a decision.
LOGIC (connector). He studied day and night; ___, he failed the exam. (a) therefore (b) because (c) however (d) moreover
(c) however
The two ideas contrast: effort versus failure.
LOGIC (cause). The flight was delayed ___ heavy fog. (a) because (b) due to (c) although (d) so
(b) due to
A noun phrase (heavy fog) follows, so “due to”.
TypeFirst checkTypical traps
Tensetime words (since, yesterday, by the time)present perfect vs simple past
Agreementreal subject, “of” phrases, along withnearest noun trap
Prepositionfixed pairs (good at, fond of)in/on/at, since/for
Articlesound of next word, “the” for known nounsan university
Vocabularypositive or negative moodsimilar-looking words (affect/effect)
Connectorrelation: contrast, cause, resultalthough … but

Shortcuts and tricks

  • Spend the first 5 seconds on the sentence, not the options.
  • If an option makes the sentence ungrammatical, strike it and do not look again.
  • Choose the simplest correct option; exam setters rarely hide the answer in a rare word.
  • Take timed sets of 10 questions in 4 minutes 10 seconds.

Common mistakes

  • Spending 40 seconds on one item.
  • Choosing a grammatically right option that changes the meaning.
  • Changing a correct answer after a second look without a reason.

VERBAL ABILITY · NEW PATTERN TASK 2 · MUST-DO

Passage Recall

Passage Recall is a memory-plus-typing task. A short passage stays on screen for about 30 seconds, then disappears; you have about 90 seconds to type what you remember. There are 4 such tasks. Copy the facts, not the exact words: accuracy of key facts and clear writing matter more than word-for-word copying.
Timeline of one task.
Group the facts into 3 boxes while reading. Names and numbers go in first.

The method

  • Second 0–5: skim for the topic: who and what.
  • Second 5–25: pick out names, numbers, dates, places and put them in 3 chunks (who · when/where · what).
  • Second 25–30: repeat the numbers silently once.
  • Write immediately when the passage disappears: start with the sentence you remember best.
  • Keep the same order as the passage; use short sentences.
  • Use exact numbers and names. If unsure, skip the detail; do not invent.
  • Spend the last 10 seconds fixing spelling and punctuation.
Typing speed (words per minute)Words you can type in 90 seconds
20 wpmabout 30 words
25 wpmabout 38 words
30 wpmabout 45 words
40 wpmabout 60 words
50 wpmabout 75 words
60 wpmabout 90 words

The practice passages below have 30 to 40 words. At 30 wpm you can type about 45 words in 90 seconds, so you must shorten sentences while keeping every fact. At 40 wpm you can type about 60 words, more than any practice passage here.

Practice passages with key facts and a model recall

Passage 1 (34 words): Riya, a software engineer from Pune, joined Zenith Tech on 3 March. She will work in the cloud team led by Mr Kapoor. Her first project is a billing app due in 6 weeks.
Key facts: Riya · software engineer · Pune · Zenith Tech · 3 March · cloud team · Mr Kapoor · billing app · 6 weeks
Model recall (34 words): Riya, a software engineer from Pune, joined Zenith Tech on 3 March. She will work in the cloud team led by Mr Kapoor. Her first project is a billing app due in 6 weeks.
Passage 2 (31 words): The annual science fair will be held on 14 December at Greenfield School. Over 40 teams from 12 schools will take part. The winning team will receive a trophy and ₹25,000.
Key facts: 14 December · Greenfield School · 40 teams · 12 schools · trophy · ₹25,000
Model recall (27 words): The annual science fair is on 14 December at Greenfield School. Over 40 teams from 12 schools will take part. The winner gets a trophy and ₹25,000.
Passage 3 (30 words): A new metro line between Airport and Central Station opens on 1 July. It has 9 stations and cuts travel time from 55 to 30 minutes. Tickets start at ₹20.
Key facts: Airport · Central Station · 1 July · 9 stations · 55 · 30 minutes · ₹20
Model recall (30 words): A new metro line from Airport to Central Station opens on 1 July. It has 9 stations and cuts travel time from 55 to 30 minutes. Tickets start at ₹20.
Passage 4 (33 words): Dr Mehta's clinic is open Monday to Saturday from 9 am to 1 pm and 5 pm to 8 pm. It is closed on Sundays. Appointments can be booked by phone or app.
Key facts: Monday to Saturday · 9 am to 1 pm · 5 pm to 8 pm · closed on Sundays · phone or app
Model recall (29 words): Dr Mehta's clinic is open Monday to Saturday, 9 am to 1 pm and 5 pm to 8 pm. It is closed on Sundays. Book by phone or app.

How to score yourself

ScoreHowTarget
Fact scorekey facts you wrote correctly ÷ total key facts (list is given for every passage)70% or more
Accuracywrong or invented facts (each costs a fact)0 invented facts
Spellingnumber of spelling slips in your answer0 to 2
Claritycomplete sentences, same orderall four tasks

The exact marking rule of the actual test is not public. This self-score is a practice tool to show where you lose facts, not an official rubric.

Shortcuts and tricks

  • Turn numbers into a small story: “3 March, 6 weeks”.
  • Make a picture for names and places.
  • Practise on different topics: notices, news, instructions, processes.
  • Type for 10 minutes every day; speed gives you time to include more facts.

Common mistakes

  • Trying to memorise word for word.
  • Writing long sentences and running out of time.
  • Adding details that were not in the passage.
  • Changing numbers (₹25,000 written as ₹2,500).

Practice set: Recall drills (read 30 s, write 90 s)

1.Read for 30 s, hide it, write in 90 s: Last quarter, the company's sales rose by 12 percent to ₹48 crore. The growth came mainly from online orders, which doubled. The CEO plans to open two new offices in Chennai and Hyderabad.Medium
2.Read for 30 s, hide it, write in 90 s: Arjun lost his wallet on the 8:15 bus to Jaipur. A passenger named Sana found it and handed it to the driver. Arjun collected it the next day from the depot, with all ₹3,500 intact.Medium
3.Read for 30 s, hide it, write in 90 s: The library will remain closed from 20 to 24 January for stock checking. Members may return books in the drop box. Late fees will not be charged for that period.Medium
4.Read for 30 s, hide it, write in 90 s: The city council has approved a plan to plant 5,000 trees along the ring road by October. Volunteers from 15 colleges will help. Each tree will be tagged with a QR code so citizens can track its growth.Advanced
5.Read for 30 s, hide it, write in 90 s: Sunrise Foods will open a new plant in Nashik in 2026 with an investment of ₹120 crore. The plant will employ 450 people and produce 30 tonnes of snacks a day. Production is expected to start in the third quarter.Advanced
6.Read for 30 s, hide it, write in 90 s: Ananya reached the office at 9:40 and found that the server was down. She informed the IT team, who restored it by 11:15. The delay affected three client calls, which were moved to the afternoon.Advanced
15
VERBAL ABILITY · NEW PATTERN TASK 3 · MUST-DO

Email Writing

The third task is a timed email of about 9 minutes. You get a short work-related situation and must write a clear, polite and well-organised email. A good email has a purpose in the first sentence, enough detail to act on, correct grammar and a courteous close. Prepare templates now so that on the day only the details change.
Seven parts of a formal email. Follow this order every time.
Use the first minute and a half to plan: who, why, what you want, by when.

What a good email contains

  • Subject line (5–8 words) that states the purpose.
  • Greeting: Dear Mr/Ms + surname, or Dear Team / Dear Sir or Madam when the name is unknown.
  • Purpose in sentence 1: “I am writing to …”.
  • Body: the reason, the key facts (dates, numbers, names), and what you have done or will do.
  • Clear request or next step with a time: “by Friday”.
  • Polite closing and sign-off: Yours sincerely (name known), Yours faithfully (name unknown), Regards / Best regards (neutral).
  • Length: roughly 80 to 150 words; short paragraphs.
  • Formal tone: no slang, no abbreviations (don’t, ASAP), no emoji, no capital-letter shouting.
Instead ofWriteWhy
I want leaveI would like to request leavepolite
Do it fastKindly complete it at the earliestpolite request
You didn’t replyI have not yet received a replyneutral, not blaming
Sorry for the problemI apologise for the inconvenience causedformal
Tell mePlease let me know / Kindly confirmpolite request
asapat the earliest / by Fridayspecific

Phrase bank

PurposeUseful phrases
OpeningI am writing to … · I am writing regarding … · With reference to …
RequestCould you please … · I would be grateful if you could … · Kindly …
ApologyI sincerely apologise for … · I regret the delay · Please accept my apologies
ComplaintI am disappointed to inform you … · I request an immediate resolution
InformationPlease find attached … · I am pleased to inform you that …
Follow-upI am following up on … · As discussed in today’s meeting …
ClosingThank you for your time. · I look forward to your reply. · Please let me know if you need any further information.

Eight model emails

Each body below is between 50 and 85 words (counted by code) so it can be typed in the available time. Change the facts, keep the structure.

Request for leave
Subject: Application for Leave on 12 and 13 March
Dear Mr Sharma,

I am writing to request leave on 12 and 13 March because I have to attend a family function in my hometown. I have completed my pending tasks and handed over the ongoing work to my colleague, Neha Rao, who will manage it in my absence. I will remain available by phone for any urgent matter. I would be grateful if you could approve my request.

Thank you for your consideration.
Yours sincerely,
Anil Verma
Body: 66 words
Complaint about a service
Subject: Complaint Regarding Delayed Delivery of Order 4821
Dear Customer Support Team,

I placed order number 4821 on 3 June, and it was promised for delivery within three days. It is now ten days later and the package has not arrived. I have contacted your helpline twice, but the problem is still unresolved. Please arrange delivery within two working days or issue a full refund. I would appreciate a written update on the status of my order.

I look forward to your prompt reply.
Regards,
Priya Nair
Body: 65 words
Follow-up after a meeting
Subject: Follow-up: Action Items from Today’s Project Meeting
Dear Team,

Thank you for attending today’s meeting. I would like to confirm the action items we agreed on. Rahul will share the revised design by Wednesday, Meena will complete testing by Friday, and I will update the client on Monday. Please let me know if I have missed anything or if any deadline needs to change.

Thank you for your support.
Best regards,
Sanjay Iyer
Body: 55 words
Request for information
Subject: Request for Details of the Data Analytics Course
Dear Admissions Team,

I am a final-year engineering student and I am interested in your six-month Data Analytics course. Could you please share the course fee, the schedule of classes and the eligibility criteria? I would also like to know whether a certificate is provided on completion. A brief reply with these details will help me decide before the registration date.

Thank you for your time.
Sincerely,
Kavya Menon
Body: 58 words
Apology for a delay
Subject: Apology for Delay in Submitting the Quarterly Report
Dear Ms Gupta,

I apologise for the delay in submitting the quarterly report, which was due on Monday. The delay was caused by a data issue that required extra verification. I have now completed the report and attached it to this email. I will make sure that I share my work earlier in future so that such delays do not occur again.

Thank you for your understanding.
Yours sincerely,
Rohan Das
Body: 59 words
Introduction and job application
Subject: Application for the Software Trainee Position
Dear Hiring Manager,

I am writing to apply for the Software Trainee position advertised on your website. I have recently completed my B.Tech in Computer Science and have built two projects in Java and SQL. I am a quick learner and enjoy teamwork. I have attached my resume for your review and would welcome the chance to discuss my application.

Thank you for considering my application.
Yours faithfully,
Meera Joshi
Body: 57 words
Reminder / payment follow-up
Subject: Reminder: Payment of Invoice 1057 Due on 20 July
Dear Mr Khan,

This is a gentle reminder that the payment for invoice 1057, amounting to ₹45,000, is due on 20 July. I have attached a copy of the invoice for your convenience. If the payment has already been made, please ignore this message and accept my thanks. Kindly let me know if you need any clarification.

Thank you for your cooperation.
Kind regards,
Vikram Patel
Body: 54 words
Thank-you and feedback
Subject: Thank You for the Training Session
Dear Mr Singh,

Thank you for conducting the training session on time management yesterday. The practical examples were very useful, and the checklist you shared has already helped me plan my week better. I would also like to suggest that a follow-up session be organised for the whole team. Please accept my sincere thanks for your effort.

Warm regards,
Divya Rao
Body: 54 words

Quick self-check (30 seconds)

CheckYes / No
Subject line present and specific
Greeting and sign-off with name
Purpose stated in the first sentence
Every fact from the question used (names, dates, numbers)
One clear request or next step
Polite and formal tone
No spelling or punctuation errors

Shortcuts and tricks

  • Keep ready one template per situation: request, complaint, apology, follow-up, information, application.
  • Use the facts given in the question; do not invent names, amounts or dates.
  • Write short sentences; long sentences cause errors.
  • If time runs low, finish with a one-line polite closing and your name.
  • Type 10 minutes a day: speed gives you room to check.

Common mistakes

  • Starting with a long background before stating the purpose.
  • Using informal words (hi, thanks a lot, gonna).
  • Forgetting the subject line or the sign-off.
  • Writing one huge paragraph.
  • Using the wrong ending (“Yours faithfully” with a named person).

Practice set: Email practice prompts (9 minutes each)

1.Write to your manager requesting two days of leave next week for a family event; say who will cover your work.Basic
2.Write to a vendor about a late delivery of office chairs ordered on 5 May; ask for delivery in three days.Basic
3.Write to your team after a meeting to confirm three action items with deadlines.Medium
4.Write to a college asking for the fee structure and last date of a certificate course.Medium
5.Apologise to a client for missing a deadline and give a new date.Medium
6.Write to HR to apply for an internship and attach your resume.Advanced
7.Politely remind a client that an invoice of ₹30,000 is overdue by one week.Advanced

VERBAL ABILITY · FINAL CHAPTER

Typing, Strategy, Formula Sheet and Mini Test

Two of the three new-pattern tasks (passage recall and email) need fast, accurate typing. This chapter gives a typing routine, a plan for the whole section, a one-page rules sheet, and a 20-question mini test in the style of Task 1.

Typing speed and accuracy

Formulas

  • Words per minute (wpm) = (characters typed ÷ 5) ÷ minutes. Example: 600 characters in 3 minutes = (600 ÷ 5) ÷ 3 = 40 wpm.
  • Accuracy % = correct characters ÷ total characters × 100.
  • Aim: 30 wpm with 95% accuracy as the minimum; 40 wpm is comfortable.
  • Daily practice: 5 minutes of copying a passage + 5 minutes of writing an email from memory.
  • Posture: wrists straight, eyes on the screen, use all ten fingers.

Plan for the whole Verbal section

TaskCount and timeWhat to do
1. Sentence completion20 items, ~25 s each (~8 min 20 s)Routine: read, type the blank, eliminate, choose. Never leave blank.
2. Passage recall4 tasks, 30 s read + 90 s write each (8 min)Chunk facts, write fast, keep numbers exact.
3. Email writing1 task, about 9 minutesPlan 1.5 min, write 6 min, check 1.5 min.
Totalabout 26 minutesPractise each task separately, then together.

The timings above follow the new Verbal pattern as described in this series; check the latest TCS notice for any change before the test.

One-page rules sheet

TopicRemember
Tensessince + point, for + period; by the time → past perfect; if + present → will
Agreementeach / every / neither + singular; along with ignored; nearer subject for either-or
Articlesa/an by sound; the with superlatives and known nouns; few = almost none, a few = some
Prepositionsin-on-at funnel; since/for; between/among; fixed pairs (fond of, good at)
Pronounsafter prepositions use me/him; than I (am); who/whom/whose
Comparisonthan with comparatives; the + superlative; to after senior/junior/prefer
Conditionalszero/first/second/third; if I were; had + V3 inversion
Voice and speechbe + V3; tense steps back; questions lose inversion
Vocabularyroots (bene, mal, spect); tone; confusing pairs
Idiomslearn by verb group; replace with plain meaning
Error spottingagreement → tense → pronoun → preposition → parallel → word choice
Recallwho, when/where, what; exact numbers; same order
Emailsubject, greeting, purpose, body, request, closing, sign-off

Five-week plan

WeekFocus
1Tenses, agreement, articles, prepositions (10 questions a day)
2Pronouns, conjunctions, comparison, conditionals, voice and speech
3Vocabulary, idioms, error spotting; start passage recall (2 a day)
4Timed sentence-completion sets; email templates (1 a day)
5Full section practice: 20 + 4 + 1 in one sitting; review mistakes

Mini test: Sentence Completion (20 items, 25 seconds each)

Mixed mini test

1.Neither the teacher nor the students ___ present yesterday. (a) was (b) were (c) is (d) has been
2.She has lived in Nagpur ___ five years. (a) since (b) for (c) from (d) in
3.The committee ___ its decision yesterday. (a) announced (b) announce (c) announcing (d) have announced
4.He is ___ honest man. (a) a (b) an (c) the (d) no article
5.If I ___ rich, I would travel the world. (a) am (b) was (c) were (d) will be
6.The report must be submitted ___ Monday at the latest. (a) in (b) at (c) by (d) since
7.The manager praised the team ___ their hard work. (a) for (b) of (c) with (d) at
8.Choose the synonym of “abundant”. (a) scarce (b) plentiful (c) weak (d) hidden
9.Choose the antonym of “expand”. (a) grow (b) shrink (c) increase (d) spread
10.He ___ the offer because the pay was low. (a) turned up (b) turned down (c) turned on (d) turned in
11.Hardly had she reached the station ___ the train left. (a) than (b) when (c) then (d) that
12.The new policy will ___ all employees. (a) effect (b) affect (c) infect (d) defect
13.This is the ___ of all the options. (a) good (b) better (c) best (d) well
14.He suggested that the meeting ___ postponed. (a) is (b) be (c) was (d) being
15.The audience ___ the speaker with a long applause. (a) welcomed (b) welcoming (c) welcome to (d) has welcome
16.She is fond ___ classical music. (a) at (b) of (c) with (d) to
17.The project was completed ahead of schedule; ___, the client was pleased. (a) however (b) therefore (c) although (d) unless
18.Passive of “They are building a bridge.” (a) A bridge is built. (b) A bridge is being built. (c) A bridge was built. (d) A bridge has been built.
19.She said, “I have finished.” → She said that she ___. (a) has finished (b) had finished (c) finished (d) was finished
20.One who knows everything is called ___. (a) omnipresent (b) omniscient (c) optimist (d) orator

Shortcuts and tricks

  • Take the mini test with a timer: 8 minutes 20 seconds total.
  • Score: 18+ excellent, 14–17 good, below 14 revise the grammar chapters.
  • Write each wrong answer in the error log with the rule.
